member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Audio.FlashlightClick
member.summary: The flashlight's switch: a short mechanical click, made here rather than taken from the game.

remarks.para: Not retail. The original has no flashlight and so no sound for one; borrowing a menu or weapon cue would sound like the thing it was borrowed from. A tail-cap switch is a few events a few milliseconds apart -- the thumb landing on the boot, the plunger bottoming out, the latch snapping over -- and what is synthesised is those events and nothing else.

Each event is a sub-millisecond burst of noise struck through a small bank of resonances, not a tone. The first version rang each event as a clean sine with one overtone, and a click with a pitch sounds like a toy: a real switch's parts are small, stiff and damped by the hand, so their modes are inharmonic, broad and gone in a few milliseconds, and what the ear hears is the edge and the colour, never a note. Under the snap sits a soft, low knock of the thumb on the rubber boot and the body of the torch.

On and off are separate sounds, as a clicky switch really is two different mechanisms: switching on is press, bottom out and latch; switching off is a softer press and the latch releasing on the way back up. Deterministic: fixed-seed generators, so every run clicks the same and nothing depends on the clock.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Audio.HitSounds
member.summary: The remastered crosshair's sounds: what a hit and a kill play.

remarks.para: Not retail, as the crosshair's marks are not: synthesised here, from nothing of any game's. Each is a pool of variants a sound is drawn from at random, so a burst never repeats itself. A hit plays a tick -- a broad click falling into a low thud near seventy hertz, gone in a fifth of a second -- and a kill a heavier confirm: a high hiss gathering for a tenth of a second into a broad impact, a deep boom under it and a faint high tail. Either plays the round's strike with it: a brighter, shorter thwack into a lower thud, and a quiet wet splatter of grainy noise.
names a folder of recordings standing in for these, laid out the same way, for judging them against a reference by ear; nothing of such a folder ships.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Audio.LampSounds
member.summary: What the level's lamps sound like coming on and going off, made here rather than taken from the game.

remarks.para: Not retail. The original's lamps never change, so it has no sound for one changing. Each sound is one of the things a real fitting does audibly, and is played at the instant has the light do it, so what is heard is the light's own sequence: a cold tube's starter ticking for each blink it makes, then the ballast taking the load; a sodium lantern's ignitor crackling, sometimes twice, then the arc catching with a soft thump and a hum.

Built from two ingredients. Mechanical and electrical events -- a contact opening, a spark -- are bursts of noise a fraction of a millisecond long, struck through a few broad resonances, as the flashlight's click is (see ): a click with a pitch sounds like a toy. Ballasts are magnetic, and hum at twice the mains frequency with a ladder of harmonics the steel's magnetostriction adds, which is made by soft-clipping a hundred-hertz tone rather than by adding clean partials -- the clipping is where the buzz comes from.

None of them loops. A ballast hums all night, but forty of them humming at once across a yard is a drone over the whole mission; what is heard here is the hum swelling as the load comes on and settling back under the ambience. Deterministic: fixed-seed generators, so every run sounds the same.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Audio.RainAmbience
member.summary: The weather, heard: six taps on one rain recording, placed around the listener's head and mixed from what measures about the building they are standing in.

remarks.para: The idea. Rain is not a sound source, it is a field — it arrives from every direction at once, and what a building does to it is not to turn it down but to reshape it. Standing in a yard you are inside the field. Step into a shed and the field is replaced by three quite different sounds arriving from three different places: the drumming of the drops on the roof over your head, the dull broadband push of the same rain through the walls, and — if a door is open — the rain itself, unfiltered, from exactly where the door is. Cross-fading a stereo loop against a quieter stereo loop reproduces none of that, which is why an interior in most games sounds like an exterior with the fader down.

What is built instead. One emitter on each of the six world axes, three metres out, moving with the listener. The probe reports how open each of those six directions is; that number decides both how loud that emitter is and how bright, and the three components above fall out of it without being special-cased:

item.description: the part of a direction that is open carries the recording untouched, at an amplitude equal to the square root of how open it is — because open-ness is a fraction of the field's power, and amplitude is the square root of power. A doorway subtends a large fraction of the sphere when you are standing in it and a tiny one from the back of the room, so a door gets louder as you approach it with no distance term written anywhere;
the upward emitter carries, in addition, the drumming — louder than the walls and brighter, scaled by how closely the roof stands over the ear.

remarks.para: The three are summed as powers, not amplitudes, because they are uncorrelated; the emitter's cutoff is their power-weighted mean in log frequency, so an emitter that is mostly doorway sounds like a doorway and one that is mostly wall sounds like a wall. Nothing in here tests "am I indoors": there is no such flag, and an awning, a doorway, a courtyard and a cellar are all just different numbers coming out of the same six.

Why six emitters and not a stereo bed. Because the request the whole design answers is "one ear at the open door and the other not", and only a real position can do that. The emitters are placed in world space around the ear, so turning the head swings the door across the stereo image exactly as it should, and under snd_3d the backend's own panning — head-related, on a device that offers it — does the work rather than a hand-written pan.

member.remarks: Close, because these are directions rather than objects: the loudness is already decided by the mix and must not be decided a second time by distance. Standing inside is what keeps the device's linear fade at unity.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Audio.VehicleSoundPlayer
member.summary: Every sound a vehicle makes: its engine sound set, its guns' reports and its turrets' traverse.

remarks.para: The engine set. A car instantiates the set its physics record names (+610) as a child of itself (0x42E320 through 0x4E6B00) while its "Play sound" holds; a helicopter instantiates helicopter_1 (0x4316D0) and a plane su27 (0x433690). Each sound of the set asks the vehicle for its parameters every tick (0x42F850, 0x432BB0, 0x434A30): the throttle, whether the engine is driving, and -- a car only -- the speed. A DefineGraph loops with its gain and pitch read off two eleven-point curves of its parameter (0x4EAEB0, 0x4E7030); a DefineTriggerOnce plays once each time its parameter turns true (0x4EA040). The T80's t80_sounds is defined by no retail script, so a tank's hull is silent.

The guns follow Gun_Fire (0x478BA0). A row of at most one round a burst plays one of its two sounds at random for each round. A longer burst starts its first sound when the hold begins -- the T80 cannon's rpg_launch_1, the M2HB's m2hb_loop -- and, when the hold ends, stops it and plays the second (rpg_launch_1 again, m2hb_loop_e). A one-shot that ends while the hold lasts is not restarted. The mount's traverse loop (tank_turret) sounds while the gun is still turning to its aim (0x46F390).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.DefaultBinds
member.summary: The keys the game binds for itself when the player has not bound them to something else.

remarks.para: Data rather than a run of if statements at start-up, because there is a rule about what may go in here and a rule is only worth having if something checks it: a default bind must not write a setting the game saves. These keys exist to flip between two implementations while looking at the same frame, and a key pressed to look at something must not decide what the game starts as tomorrow.

That is not hypothetical. r_rt was archived while F6 toggled it, so comparing the hardware and software trace once wrote the software path into settings.cfg: the next launch came up on it, the graphics preset read as Custom because a managed value no longer matched, and the picture was quietly worse with nothing on screen to say why. The setting is no longer archived, and DefaultBindTests is what stops the next one being.

member.remarks: Deliberately only understands toggle. A bind that runs anything else is not making a setting follow a key press and has nothing for the rule above to check.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostConfiguration
member.summary: Reads and writes the game's settings and player profiles, always leaving the original installation untouched.

remarks.para: What the player accumulates — their profiles, their settings, their progress — is written to , not into the game folder. An installation may sit somewhere the player cannot write, on a read-only mount, or be shared between several people with their own profiles, and none of those work if the game saves next to its own data.
The file is OpenIGI's own openigi-config.qvm and never the retail config.qvm, which is read but never written. The format is identical, so copying one over the other would work.

member.param: The virtual file system the installation is read through.

member.returns: The loaded configuration, or a fresh default when none can be read.
member.remarks: In order: the player's own file, then one an earlier build left inside the installation, then the retail file, then defaults. The second of those is only ever read — the next save moves it out to the per-user location, so profiles made before this moved survive rather than appearing lost.

member.summary: Gets the frame the map computer opens itself on, or 0 for never. Set by -computercam.
member.remarks: The computer's counterpart to , and a development shortcut for the same reason: opening it runs a second and a half of camera move and display boot, and a capture of that has to begin on a frame somebody can ask for again. member.remarks: + statements run at start-up, before any level exists, so they cannot reach anything a mission owns. member.summary: Gets the one graphics preset this build allows, or to let the player choose.
member.remarks: A property of the build rather than a command-line option: the browser build is held on . It is applied over any saved settings, the menu stops offering the others and gfx_preset refuses them. When set, is not read.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.CampaignMissionLimit
member.summary: Gets how many missions, counted along the campaign from its first, this build offers, or for all of them.
member.remarks: A property of the build rather than a command-line option: the browser build offers the first six. A mission past the limit is not listed, cannot be started from a save or the command line, and finishing the last one offered completes the campaign.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.MissionCycleFrames
member.summary: Gets how many frames each leg of an abandon/replay cycle lasts, or 0 for never. Set by -missioncycle.
member.remarks: A development shortcut in the same family as : leaving a mission is a teardown of every renderer and every accelerator the level built, and entering one is all of it again. Repeating the pair on a known cadence is what makes the cost of the transition, and anything it fails to release, something a run can measure rather than something a player reports.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.TitleCycleFrames
member.summary: Gets how many frames a game runs for before the next installed one is switched to.
member.remarks: Zero for never. Set by -titlecycle, and one level up: a title switch replaces the task loop, the resource registry, the mission table, the content session and every renderer together, which is the largest teardown a session performs. Until this it could only be reached by a person choosing another game from the menu, so nothing could measure it or run it often enough to see what it fails to release.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.BackdropCycleFrames
member.summary: Gets how many frames a menu backdrop is shown for before the next mission is selected.
member.remarks: on the menu's side of Play, set by -backdropcycle. A backdrop swap tears down and rebuilds every renderer, every mesh and every traced structure a level owns while the loop keeps presenting, which is a harder case than leaving a mission and had no way to be run other than clicking down the campaign list.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.PresetCycleFrames
member.summary: Gets how many frames each graphics preset is kept before the next is applied.
member.remarks: Set by -presetcycle; walks vanilla, enhanced, high and ultra in turn.

member.remarks: A tool: it builds each mission in turn, finds the places its menu backdrop should circle, writes them out and quits. What it produces is then hand-owned — see .

member.summary: Gets where to write, as JSON, the light the last frame was lit with: the sun or moon, the sky, the exposure settings and every lamp fixture as the renderer receives it. writes nothing.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.FieldOfView
member.summary: Gets a fixed horizontal field of view in degrees, or null for the game's own ninety. For lining a capture up against an external render whose camera lens differs.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.CameraEnd
member.summary: Gets the world position in metres the fly-through camera ends a flight at, or for no flight. Set by -camend; see .

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.CameraYawEnd
member.summary: Gets the yaw in radians the flight ends on, or to hold the opening yaw. Set by -yawend.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.CameraPitchEnd
member.summary: Gets the pitch in radians the flight ends on, or to hold the opening pitch. Set by -pitchend.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.FlightFrames
member.summary: Gets how many frames the flight itself takes, or to spread it over the whole capture. Set by -flightframes.
member.remarks: The frames after it hold the end pose, which is what makes a flight able to come to a stop. That matters for ghosting: a temporal filter drags a trail behind moving content, and a trail is only measurable once the motion has stopped and the picture is expected to have settled. Comparing a held frame against the same pose reached standing still measures exactly the smear and nothing else.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.FlightDelay
member.summary: Gets how many rendered frames a flight holds its start pose before it moves.
member.remarks: A flight otherwise moves from the first frame, while the level is still loading and every temporal history is empty -- so a capture of a walk measured the load, not the walk. Held this long first, the move starts from a converged frame, the way a player's does.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.CaptureRate
member.summary: Gets the frames per second a lockstep capture is rendered at, or for one frame per tick.
member.remarks: Above the simulation's own rate the synthetic clock advances by a fraction of a tick per frame and the presentation blends between ticks, as it does in play, so a 60 fps capture moves smoothly and still depends only on its arguments. Set by -capturerate.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.CameraShake
member.summary: Gets the amplitude in degrees of a per-frame camera shake laid over whatever else the camera is doing, or zero for none. Set by -camshake.
member.remarks: A smooth flight is not what a temporal filter actually has to survive. A player's view is never still and never moves evenly: it jitters by a pixel or two at a time and changes direction constantly, which is the case that breaks reprojection — a smooth pan gives every pixel the same velocity for many frames, so a history that reprojects badly still reprojects consistently. This lays a deterministic pseudo-random angular offset over the pose, so a run stays reproducible under -lockstep while the motion is no longer something the filter can settle into.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.CameraSwing
member.summary: Gets how many degrees of yaw are added on every other frame, or zero. Set by -camswing.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.HasFlight
member.summary: Gets a value indicating whether a scripted free-camera flight is asked for — an end pose the opening camera is flown to over the frame budget. When set, -screenshot writes one numbered frame per rendered frame rather than a single still, so the in-motion behaviour of the temporal filters is visible in the sequence.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Configuration.HostOptions.Difficulty

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Content.ContentLayers
member.summary: Works out the stack of content layers one title runs with.

remarks.para: Highest priority first:

item.description: every -content folder, in the order named (development);
the folder in OPENIGI_OVERRIDES, if set and there is NO profile (the launcher's old hand-off, kept so scripts and shortcuts that set it still work);
the data of the mods played, the last in their order first (IGameTitleRuntime.ContentFolders);
the content profile's list for this title, which is the player's load order and holds the game folder's own overrides as one entry among the packs;

remarks.para: With no profile, or a profile that does not mention this title, the third part is the game folder's own overrides alone -- the behaviour from before there were packs.

The legacy folder is ignored whenever a profile is in force. The launcher sets both on purpose, because it may start a build from before profiles, which reads only OPENIGI_OVERRIDES; a build that reads the profile must not also stack that folder, or the pack the old build was given would sit above the player's whole order, and win even when it is switched off.
Re-run on every title switch, because each game has its own list and its own data root.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.CommandPaletteBody
member.summary: A fuzzy finder over every command and variable, opened with a chord and dismissed by choosing.

remarks.para: The same registries the prompt completes against, reached without typing a prompt line first. The difference is intent: the prompt is for composing a statement, the palette is for finding one thing and running it. So it opens centred and modal-feeling, shows more of each entry, and closes the moment something is chosen.

A chosen command runs; a chosen variable is placed in the prompt with a trailing space instead. Running a bare variable name only prints it, and silently printing something is a poor answer to a reader who went looking for it — they almost always meant to set it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.ConsoleBody
member.summary: The developer console's contents: a filter bar, the scrollback, the prompt, and the completion list floating over them.

remarks.para: The log draws through a , so a full four-thousand-line scrollback costs the same as an empty one. The prompt is drawn directly rather than being a widget: it needs a caret at an arbitrary index, a selection wash, per-token syntax colouring and an inline ghost completion, none of which the shared text field has any business knowing about.

Every measurement comes from the theme's spacing unit and character cell, and everything that lands on screen is rounded to a whole pixel. Half-pixel text and half-pixel hairlines are most of what separates an interface that looks designed from one that looks approximate.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.CVarBrowserBody
member.summary: A live table of every console variable: filtered as the reader types, showing value, default, flags and help, and editable in place.

remarks.para: The registry holds around a hundred variables and cvarlist prints all of them into a log that then has to be scrolled. A table that narrows as you type answers "what is this called" and "what is it set to" in one place, which is the question the log was a poor answer to.

Editing happens in the row. Copying a name to the prompt and typing a value there works, but it puts the value being changed and the value it had on different parts of the screen. Editing in place keeps them together, and a rejected value can be reported against the row that refused it.

member.summary: The developer console's own console variables.

remarks.para: Declared in the desktop application rather than beside the renderer's, because they configure a tool that only the desktop shell has. The application already references the CVar source generator as an analyzer, so the module initialiser that forces these declarations to register is emitted here as it is for every other container — but must still call it explicitly before the settings file is read, or a saved con_ line would be met with "unknown variable" and the reader's layout would silently never come back.
Everything here is , because every one of them is a preference a reader sets once and expects to find again. None is a cheat and none affects the simulation.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.DevConsoleCVars.Scale
member.summary: How large the developer tools draw, as a multiple of real pixels.

remarks.para: The console sizes itself in back-buffer pixels rather than the shell's 16:9 design units, so a wider display shows more console rather than a larger one — which is what a tool wants and what a menu does not.

Resolution is a different question from aspect ratio, though, and raw pixels get that one wrong: the same panel on a 4K monitor would be half the physical size it is on a 1080p one of the same width. So a factor derived from the display height is applied underneath, and this is the reader's multiplier on top of it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.DevConsoleLayout
member.summary: Serialises where the developer tools' panels sit, so a reader's arrangement survives a restart.

remarks.para: The whole layout is one string variable — console:40,40,1200,620,1,0|cvars:… — rather than five numbers per panel. settings.cfg records every archived variable that differs from its default, and thirty geometry numbers would bury the registry that find and cvarlist exist to make searchable.

Parsing never throws and never rejects the whole string. A layout is written by a tool and may be hand-edited, may come from an older build with different panels, and may name a panel this build no longer has. Any segment that does not make sense is skipped and its panel falls back to its default position; a reader who mangles one entry does not lose the rest of their arrangement.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.DevConsolePanels
member.summary: The developer console's panels: the windows, the bodies inside them, and the handful of things that open, close and pin them.

remarks.para: Shared by the console's drawing, its pointer, its keys and its commands, which all need to ask the same questions — is the variable browser showing, which window is the palette — of the same set. Holding the set in one place is what lets each of those live in its own class without four copies of the window fields drifting apart.

Everything here is empty until runs, which happens only once the display exists. The commands are registered long before that, so the requests that arrive early — and — are held here and applied later.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.DevConsoleTheme
member.summary: The developer tools' palette, type scale and spacing rhythm.

remarks.para: Wraps a rather than extending it. The elevation, selection and status roles belong to any modern surface and live on the shared theme where every widget can reach them; a colour for "a token that turned out to be an alias" belongs to exactly one tool.

The spacing scale is the reason the panels look like one tool. Every inset, gap and row height below comes from , so nothing is nudged by eye and no two panels drift apart. Type sizes are derived the same way from one body size, and every one of them is rounded to a whole pixel before a face is asked for — see for why that matters more than it sounds like it should.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.DeveloperConsole
member.summary: The developer console's on-screen half: a set of floating panels, the input that drives them, and the drawing.

remarks.para: Replaces the fixed half-screen drop-down the console used to be. The panels are ordinary s in a , so dragging, resizing, snapping and z-order are the framework's problem rather than this class's, and the variable browser, the watch list and the statistics panel are the same widget with different contents.

Keyboard focus follows the window in front. There is no separate focus concept: the layer already raises whatever was pressed, so the frontmost panel is the one the reader last touched, and that is the one that should receive typing. It is the rule every desktop has, and it costs nothing.

It builds its own layout context. The shell authors against a 1920×1080 reference so a menu keeps its proportions on any display; a developer tool wants the opposite — constant physical size, so the same monitor shows the same amount of text whatever the aspect ratio. Passing the real viewport as the reference makes equal con_scale alone, which turns every Px() in the widgets below into a real pixel without any of them knowing.

Input is read before it is captured. The mouse's buttons, motion and wheel all read as idle once is set, while its position deliberately keeps working. So everything is sampled first, and the capture is the last thing that happens.
This class is the coordinator. The panels themselves live in , the mouse in , typing in , the panel commands in and the overlay marks in ; each panel's own keys are handled by its body.

member.summary: Works out how much to enlarge the interface for the display it is on.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.HostConsole
member.summary: The desktop shell's console: the registry, the command set, the settings file and the on-screen view.

remarks.para: Composed once at start-up. The order matters and is the order the plan calls for: declarations are forced to register, then settings.cfg is applied over the defaults, then the command line's + statements are applied over that. So a command line always wins for the session, and what it put in place is what gets saved — which is what a player switching to +gfx_preset ultra once and then never passing it again expects.
Everything the game writes through is mirrored into the scrollback, so opening the console shows the log rather than an empty panel.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.IWorldInspector.TryProject(System.Int32,OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.ScreenMarker@)
member.summary: Projects an entity to where it appears on screen.
member.param: The entity's handle.
Receives where it lands and how far away it is.
member.returns: when the entity exists and could be projected.

remarks.para: Screen space rather than a world-space wireframe, and deliberately so. There is no debug-line renderer and the 2D painter has no line primitive, so a real box would be a new render path; but more importantly a marker drawn in the interface pass is over the scene, which is exactly what "visible through a wall" means. A world-space box would need a depth-test toggle to achieve the same thing.

The point may land outside the viewport, or behind the camera entirely. Both are reported rather than refused, so the caller can pin the marker to the nearest edge and point at it — which is what keeps a selection findable once the reader has turned away from it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.LogSelection
member.summary: A range of scrollback text picked out with the pointer, from one row and column to another.

remarks.para: Held as an anchor and a focus rather than a start and an end, for the same reason a text field is: the anchor is where the drag began and stays put, the focus follows the pointer, and dragging upwards works without the two ever swapping roles.

Rows are indexed among the lines currently passing the filter, not into the scrollback. That is what makes a selection behave as it looks — dragging across three visible lines selects those three, not whatever happens to sit between them in the unfiltered buffer. It also means a selection does not survive a filter change, which is why one clears it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.MonoFontSet
member.summary: The developer tools' fixed-pitch faces, rasterised once per pixel size actually drawn.

remarks.para: Why a set rather than one font. A coverage atlas is a bitmap: drawn at the size it was rasterised at, each texel lands on one pixel and the text is as crisp as the rasteriser made it. Drawn at any other size it is resampled through a linear filter, and minification in particular turns stems grey and closes counters — a 32-pixel atlas drawn at 13 is being shrunk to 40%, which is enough to make a capital L read as an I and an E as an F.

So each size the interface asks for gets its own atlas at exactly that height, and every draw is one-to-one. The cost is bounded and small: the tools use three or four sizes, each is a few hundred kilobytes, and keys on the pixel height so every one of them is rasterised once ever and read from disk afterwards.
Sizes are rounded to whole pixels before being asked for, both because a fractional atlas height would defeat the caching and because half-pixel text is the other half of why small type looks soft.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.PromptEditor
member.summary: The developer console's typing: the held-key repeaters, the blinking caret, the clipboard, and the edits every panel's text field shares.

remarks.para: One instance serves every panel, and that is deliberate rather than convenient. The repeaters keep their own timing, so the arrow a reader is holding goes on repeating at the same cadence whichever panel happens to be in front when the frame reads it — exactly as it did when they all lived on the console itself.
The caret blinks here because typing is what resets it: any edit restarts the cycle with the caret showing, so it never vanishes in the middle of a word.

remarks.para: Drawn in the interface pass, over the scene, which is what makes it visible through a wall with no depth-test trickery — and the reason this is a screen-space bracket rather than a world-space box.

The bracket shrinks with distance but never below a size that can be seen, so something a kilometre away is still a mark rather than a pixel. When it leaves the viewport the mark pins to the nearest edge and becomes an arrow pointing at it, so a selection is never simply lost the moment the reader turns around.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.WatchBody
member.summary: The pinned-value panel: a short list of names and whatever they read this frame.

remarks.para: Re-read every frame it draws, because that is the entire point — a value you have to ask for again is a value you cannot watch change. The list is short by nature, so it is drawn directly rather than through the virtualised table; a reader who pins forty things has already lost the thread.
This is one of the two panels that can outlive the console being shut, which is why it must cost almost nothing: the entries are read into a list it owns rather than allocated per frame.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.DevTools.WorldInspector
member.summary: The game's answer to the developer inspector: everything the world is made of, and how to go and look at it.

remarks.para: Its own type over , which is what the host shows it: the scene, the soldiers, the mission's registries, the player, the camera and the terrain.

Handles encode their source. An index into the last list produced would come apart the moment the filter changed between listing and asking for detail, so a handle is kind × + index and resolves on its own. That is what lets the panel keep a selection while the reader types in the filter box.

Everything crosses as a snapshot or a string. The panels are on the far side of an interface that must not see gameplay types, and a panel holding a live placement across a mission change would be holding one the loader had already discarded.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Diagnostics.PresentationPacingProbe
member.summary: Measures whether presented motion advances in step with real time, when the Pacing log category is at Debug.

remarks.para: Frame rate is not smoothness. What the eye reads as judder is the presented simulation clock advancing unevenly against the wall clock: a frame that covers twice as much sim time as the one before it reads as a stutter however fast the frames arrive. Every frame the renderer decides where it sits between two ticks, so the pair (tick count, blend) IS the sim clock the picture is drawn at, exact to the fraction.

The metric is the ratio of sim time advanced to wall time elapsed, per frame. A perfectly paced run holds it at 1: the picture moves one millisecond of animation for every millisecond that passes. A spread around 1 is judder, and its width is how much. This is deliberately blind to frame rate -- an even 40 fps scores 1, an uneven 300 fps does not, which is exactly the distinction being made.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost
member.summary: The audio half of the composition root: opening the device and keeping the buses levelled.

The remastered binoculars, for whichever player looks through them: Project I.G.I.'s through its viewpoint, or a title's player through . One lens, one interface () and one highlight (), whichever title's player it is.
Skipping a cutscene: the break key held until the ring in the corner fills.
The display settings: the window's mode and size, the API drawing into it, and the frame-rate cap.
The frame loop's passes, in the order runs them.
The language the game's text is read in, and changing it while the game runs.

remarks.para: Every language is a folder of archives whose keys carry the language's name (), so a language is changed by unregistering one folder's archives and registering another's, and pointing the string table at the new name. Nothing is rebuilt: the menus, the campaign list and a mission's computer all look their keys up as they draw.

Two registries can be holding the text: the title's, which the menus' string table reads, and the played mission's, which a menu backdrop brought with it when it was promoted. A backdrop built before the change was built with the old language's archives, so a promotion mounts the current one into it too ().

member.summary: -dumplighting: the light a frame was lit with, written out so an external render can be set up from the same numbers.

remarks.para: A second derivation of the sun, the moon or a lamp's strength on the other side would drift the moment either side changed; reading what this frame actually handed the renderer cannot. Everything is in world space and metres, the frame the level is authored in, so the reader needs only a level export's pivot to place it.

Every fixture the level has is written, not only the ones this frame selected: an external render lights with all of them, and the selection is a budget of this renderer's rather than a fact about the level. Each carries the strength and reach the frame loop would give it, from the same arithmetic.

member.summary: The host's side of NVIDIA's optional features: what it asks of Reflex, and of frame generation.
member.remarks: The device decides what can run and says why when something cannot; the host only turns the settings into requests and tells the device the things only the game knows — whether this frame is gameplay at all.
member.summary: The switch between renderers: asking for it, and picking the game back up after it.
What the game does when a setting changes, and taking that back when the game ends.
What builds before its first frame, in the order it builds it.
The terrain's height raster, for the global illumination's untraced march: built off the frame loop at load, uploaded when it is ready, and handed to whichever surface-cache lighting the level has.
member.remarks: The march finds the level's placements in its distance field and nothing else; the terrain is not one of them. See .
member.summary: Changing which game the session is running, without the process restarting.

remarks.para: Everything a title owns is rebuilt; everything the session owns is kept. The window, the graphics device, the audio device, the console, the settings, the render scheduler and the wall clock belong to the process. The file system's LOCAL device, the resource registry, the task loop, the mission table, the content modules and every renderer belong to the game, and a switch replaces all of them together.

The audio device is the session's and what plays through it is the title's, which is a line worth stating because the first version of this did not draw it: the sound bank, the sound definitions and the score all read through the LOCAL device, so a switch that left them standing kept the outgoing game's menu theme playing under the incoming game's menu. is where that is put right.

The mechanism is not new. Promoting a menu backdrop into the played mission already swaps _loop, _resources and _resourceFileSystem for a set built elsewhere, and the mission preview loader already builds a complete title session off the render thread. This is that same handover with the title changed as well.

member.content: A title's own player: stood up, fed its input once a tick, and looked through.

remarks.para: Present only for a title whose composition root supplies an . Everything here is behind , which stays for a title that walks the host's own rig, so that rig's path is the one it always was.
The host's rig and a title's player are never both standing: when the title stands its own, the host's is let go and every system that reads the host's rig sees no player.

member.summary: A touch screen's controls: the fingers read once a frame and pressed as the keys the player's actions are bound to.
member.remarks: Whatever has a touch screen -- the browser build on a phone, a tablet -- reports its fingers in , and nothing is shown or pressed until the first one comes down. The keys and mouse buttons pressed are the ones the player's profile binds to each action, so a rebinding moves the button with it, and the game reads them as it reads a keyboard.
member.summary: The remaster's weapon wheel: held open on its key, steered by the mouse, and the world slowed while it is.

remarks.para: Not retail. The wheel belongs to the remastered display () and to whichever player stands in the mission, the game's own or a title's (). It opens only where the player would take the look this frame -- not in a menu, the console, a computer, a cutscene, on a ladder or dead -- and any of those taking the frame shuts it, choosing nothing.

While it is open the player is held still: the mouse steers the wheel and the keys do nothing. Time slows to as it opens and comes back as it shuts, and every sound with the music is pitched down and muffled with it (), by pushing the clock's time base on by the share of each frame not to be counted (): the schedule stretches for both games at once and nothing in either's tick changes. Not under lockstep, whose synthetic clock moves only as frames render, and they render only as ticks fall due: pushing the schedule there would hold both still for ever.

member.summary: Opens the audio output, and binds the volume variables to it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.AdvanceAudio
member.summary: Places the ear, and advances the device, the score and the weather bed, once a frame.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.UpdateListener
member.summary: Puts the listener where the player's eye is.

remarks.para: Every frame rather than every tick, and from the same blended pose the view model uses, so a source does not step across the stereo image at 30 Hz under a camera that glides. The camera already reports metres — it divides the body's engine units by 4096 — which is the unit the device works in, so nothing is converted here.

Without this, every positional sound in the game would be placed relative to a listener sitting at the world origin: distance attenuation would key off the corner of the map and the stereo image would never move.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.ResetSoundsForMission
member.summary: Empties the bank and re-mounts what does not belong to a mission.

remarks.para: Called before each mission load, so the mission's own directory is mounted into a bank holding only the menu sounds. The original rebuilds its table the same way; leaving the previous level's sounds in place would let a name resolve to a sound the new level never shipped.

Clearing is the only thing that can retire a name, because the bank keeps the FIRST mount of one — faithfully, since the original's loader reports "SOUND - File %s already loaded!" rather than replacing. Every mission ships its own sounds/game_music.wav, and a mounted entry holds the path it was found at rather than the MISSION: alias it was found through, so a bank carried across a load answers game_music with the previous level's score forever.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.MountMissionSounds(OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedMission)
member.summary: Mounts the sound directories a mission plays out of.
member.remarks: Called from BringMissionUp, which is the one place BOTH routes into a mission pass through. A cold start has already had these mounted by the mission loader and this adds nothing -- the first mount of a name wins. A mission PROMOTED from the menu's backdrop never went through that loader at all, so without this its sounds and its score are simply absent, which is exactly what pressing Play in the menu used to give: silence.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.LoadRainAmbience
member.summary: Loads the rain recording the weather bed is built from.
member.remarks: A mono 16-bit PCM WAV under Assets/sounds, prepared as a seamless loop — see the notes beside the asset. Mono is a requirement rather than a preference: only a mono source is placed in three dimensions, and placing the rain is the whole point. A missing file is not a fault; the weather simply stays silent, exactly as it did before this existed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.UpdateRainAmbience(System.Single)
member.summary: Drives the weather bed from the level the player is standing in.

remarks.para: After and from the listener's own position, so the ear the rain is measured around is the same ear everything else is heard with. Taking the eye from the camera a second time here would be one blend away from the first and would drift.

Whether it rains is the renderer's answer, not a second opinion. The level's own RainEffect task decides, through the same IsWeatherEnabled the draw path reads, so forcing the weather on from the console or the campaign screen is heard as well as seen. What must NOT be consulted is the storm's IsActive: that goes false the moment the camera is under a roof, which is precisely the case this whole system exists to sound different in rather than to fall silent in.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.SpawnBallisticImpactParticles
member.summary: Spawns the particle bursts for whatever ballistic rounds landed this tick.
member.remarks: Beside the impact sounds because it reads the same impacts and resolves the same material; a human takes the flesh burst, with no surface normal to bias it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.ResetSoundsForTitle
member.summary: Empties the bank and the score for a different game, and starts that game's theme.

remarks.para: The menu's sounds belong to the title, not to the session. Everything under menusystem/sound/ is read through LOCAL:, and a title switch re-points that device at the other installation — so a bank left standing across the switch answers every menu name with the outgoing game's sound. The bank keeps the FIRST mount of a name and reports a repeat rather than replacing it, faithfully to the original, which means re-mounting alone cannot retire anything: only clearing can.

The score has to be told as well as silenced, and for two reasons. The player treats a repeat of the playing track as a no-op so that re-entering the menu does not stutter it, so a switch that merely asked for menu_music again would be declined; and a voice already streaming holds the handle it opened, so the outgoing game's theme would go on playing under the incoming game's menu whatever the bank now says. That is the bug this exists for.

The definitions go too. They are loaded per mission from the title's own resources, and MountMissionSounds only builds a registry when there is none — so a registry carried across a switch would hand the incoming game the outgoing one's names.

remarks.para: Only for settings moved off their default: a variable sitting where it shipped is not asking for anything, and warning about it every launch would bury the ones that are. It also silently divides a comparison: two renders of "the same settings" are not the same picture if one backend honours a setting and the other drops it.

member.summary: Starts reading the two shared animation sets on a worker.

It reads files and allocates and touches nothing else in the session, so there is no reason for it to be between the player and the first frame — and at start-up the render thread is otherwise waiting on the driver to build a device, which is exactly the moment a worker is free.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.ForgetSharedAnimations
member.summary: Drops the shared sets so the next mission reads the running title's own.
member.remarks: Called when the game being played changes, which is the only thing that can invalidate them. A read still in flight is abandoned rather than waited on: it reads files and touches nothing else, so the worst it can do is finish into a task nobody holds.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.RetailAir(OpenIGI.Rendering.SceneFog)
member.summary: Gets the air the world wears when the retail fog is on, preferring the level's own.
member.param: The fog this band of Project I.G.I.'s GlobalLight publishes.
member.returns: The fog to draw into.

remarks.para: GlobalLight is the FIRST game's task, and it is the only thing the frame used to ask. So on the vanilla tier -- the one tier that fogs through rather than through the froxel volume -- I.G.I. 2's world was drawn with no fog at all: its own authored air was set once when the mission loaded and then overwritten by an empty GlobalLight on the first frame, and every frame after.

It also hid the ground's per-pass fog colour, which had nothing to tint. That is worth saying because the two faults look identical from the outside -- far hills that are not hazed -- and fixing either alone leaves the other in place.

Project I.G.I. cannot reach the new branch: ITitlePresentationProvider.ReadAtmosphere defaults to null and only the sequel answers it, so is null for the first game and this returns exactly what the frame asked for before.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.AdoptPreview(OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionPreview)
member.summary: Makes a preview built on a worker the live backdrop, doing on the render thread only what has to happen there.
member.param: The built preview, from .

remarks.para: Everything a backdrop is made of — the packs, the task tree, the scene, the collision index, the terrain surface, the level's sun, its baked probe field — arrived already built. What is left is the part that cannot leave this thread: a GL texture, buffer and framebuffer all belong to the context that made them, so the three renderers are constructed here. That is a handful of milliseconds against the several hundred the whole load used to cost the frame.

The renderers are built against the preview's OWN resource registry and file system, because a resolves models and textures through the registry it was given for as long as it lives, and the sky reads through the file system whose MISSION: alias points at this level. Holding the preview keeps both alive; dropping it drops the whole context.

A backdrop is looked at, never played, so nothing a played mission needs is set up: no nav graphs, no player, no weapons, no HUD. Drawn lite (, the default) it has no soldiers, surface cache or distance field either -- a render pass ending in a device wait and an upload that landed as the swap's stall -- and Play builds them behind the going-in sequence.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.DumpShowcasePoints(System.String,OpenIGI.Game.World.MenuStringTable)
member.summary: Builds every mission and writes out the places its menu backdrop should circle.
member.param: The file to write, in 's format.
The language table, so each entry can carry the mission's real name.
member.remarks: -poidump's body. It builds each mission the same way the menu does — the whole point being that the places written are exactly the ones the game would have found — and walks them in campaign order so the file reads down the campaign. A mission that will not build is skipped with a warning rather than taking the run down; its backdrop then finds its places at load, as it would anyway.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.ApplyLevelConstants(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask)
member.summary: Applies what a title reads off a level once and the renderer keeps for the whole of it.
member.param: The level's task tree.

remarks.para: Two title seams, both constants of the level rather than of the frame. The AIR: I.G.I. 2 reads a fog colour, a fog density and a flat ambient off its GlobalLight and fogs every surface against them; Project I.G.I. authors none of this and answers nothing, which leaves its picture exactly as it was (). The OBJECT SHADING: the sequel's bakes are MODULATE2X and its unlightmapped objects are lit by a fixed-function sun read off the level; the other title keeps , the compositing it always had. The gain and the sun's direction are the world renderer's, per draw; the sun's colours are the device's, baked in beside the fog.

Called from BOTH ways a level comes up: , where the menu builds it as a backdrop, and the cold path of . It used to live in the latter's not-promoted block alone, so a mission entered through the menu -- the way the game is played -- had no haze, white tanks and unlit objects, while one launched straight to had all three.

when the level arrived as the menu's backdrop and is being promoted rather than loaded. The backdrop is already drawn — its scene, collision index, terrain, sky, sun, grade and camera were all built by off the render thread — so the steps that would rebuild them are skipped and the rest runs exactly as it does for a cold start. The order of everything else is deliberately untouched between the two paths: the AI's ray cast closes over _mission.Terrain, the interactions have to exist before the brains are animated, and the weapon rosters have to load before humanplayer.qvm runs.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.PromoteBackdrop(OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionPreview)
member.summary: Turns the menu's backdrop into the mission being played, without loading anything.
member.param: The backdrop, which must be the mission the player asked for.
member.returns: when the mission is up and the player is standing in it.

remarks.para: The level under the menu is not a picture of the mission — it is the mission, built by on a worker thread while the player was reading the briefing. The only reason it was not playable is that it was built into its own private , which is exactly what made building it off the render thread safe: its task tree, its script namespace and its variables are unreachable from the running game, so nothing in it could ever be ticked. Promotion is the game changing which loop it advances.

What that buys is the whole of the load: the packs are parsed, the scene walked, the collision index built, the terrain surface built and — the single largest cost — every ground tile's detail map derived, all of it already done and none of it on this thread. What is left is the part that genuinely cannot leave the render thread, which is the GL uploads, and those are the subject of the arming that runs while the menu is idle.

The outgoing loop and its resource registry are dropped here. That is not housekeeping: a resource registry holds a level's worth of packs, and already carries the scar of a leak in the same shape — a world renderer dropped without being disposed leaked a level's textures per row of the mission list.

member.summary: Starts the going-in sequence and defers the load until its departure has played.

What brings the mission up: a promotion of the backdrop, or a cold start.
member.remarks: The order is the whole design. The clean picture -- the level as the player sees it now, with no interface over it -- is held on the very next frame, before the interface is drawn; the interface then leaves and the picture falls out of focus over a beat; and only then does the render thread block on the load. member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.BeginMissionWarmUp(OpenIGI.Game.World.MissionDescriptor)
member.summary: Starts holding a level back, from before its load begins until the picture it will be shown with is final.
member.param: The mission being brought up.

remarks.para: Why a load ending is not the same as a level being ready. Most of this renderer's lighting is temporal: the screen probe gather accumulates its estimate per pixel across frames, the world radiance cache fills its probes over several, the temporal resolve needs a history before it has anything to reconstruct from, and the auto-exposure adapts towards the scene rather than jumping to it. None of that can be computed in the load, because all of it is defined in terms of FRAMES -- there is no way to have a history without having drawn some. And under the real-time model the structures it lights from are built rather than switched on: a distance field that may still be baking, a surface cache that converges over dispatches.

So the level is held by until those structures exist and have converged, and then for a few frames more -- drawn as normal, with every temporal system accumulating exactly as it would in play, but with the finished picture kept off the screen. That is what every shipping game does behind a loading screen, and it is the only honest way to promise that what appears is final: the alternative is showing the player the renderer converging, which reads as the game breaking and then repairing itself.
Every route in gets : the held picture, the card, the shot over the start, the reveal. The card covers the blocking part; the shot's hold covers the lighting.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.NotifyMissionBuilt

member.summary: Abandons the warm-up, so the level is shown on the next frame.
member.remarks: For anything that takes the player out of the level before it was ever shown — abandoning to the campaign, a mission that fails during its own warm-up — where holding on would keep a card over a menu.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.ReportLoadStage
member.summary: Reports one more stage of the blocking load finished, and shows it.
member.remarks: Called from EndStage, so the fourteen named stages of bringing a mission up each move the bar by one share while the render thread is otherwise not presenting at all.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.DrawMissionWarmUp(OpenIGI.Rendering.SpriteBatch)
member.summary: Advances the hold by one drawn frame and draws the loading screen over the withheld picture.
member.param: The 2D batch, between its own begin and end.
member.returns: when the screen was drawn.
member.remarks: Drawn over a frame that was fully rendered rather than instead of one. That is the whole point: the scene has to be drawn for its temporal passes to advance, so what this does is withhold it, not skip it. Once the gate opens the sequence reveals: the card leaves and the held picture comes back into focus over the live, settled level.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.PresentLoadingFrame
member.summary: Draws and presents a single loading frame, from outside the render loop, during a blocking load.

remarks.para: Bringing a mission up is a few hundred milliseconds of work on the render thread -- uploading meshes and textures, reading nav graphs, capturing the surface cache -- and none of it presents a frame. So whatever was last on screen stayed there, frozen, and a window that stops presenting for long enough is dimmed and marked as not responding by the compositor. The loop cannot help with that: it is precisely what is blocked.

So frames are drawn and swapped by hand as each stage of the load finishes, with the same sequence the loop draws before and after -- the picture already held, the card already up -- so the load is invisible in the presentation: the bar moves and the light keeps drifting.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.LoadTitleResources
member.summary: Builds the running title's resource registry and the archives the menus resolve through.
member.remarks: The first of the two phases a title comes up in. It is separate because of when each is possible rather than for tidiness: the menus need their string table before the console, the settings and the render scheduler exist, and the task loop below cannot be built until they do. A switch runs both back to back; start-up runs them where each becomes possible.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.LoadTitleSession
member.summary: Builds the running title's task loop, mission table and content session.

remarks.para: Called once from start-up and again on every switch, which is what keeps the two honest: there is no separate boot path for a switch to drift away from. What it deliberately does NOT touch is anything the process owns — the console has already wrapped the log, the settings are loaded, the audio device is open, and none of that is a game's to replace.

The wall clock is kept too, and that is load-bearing rather than incidental: a new starts its own GameClock at tick zero, and every elapsed reading in the frame loop would jump backwards at the moment of the swap. The schedule is carried across the same way a promoted backdrop carries it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.RebuildPreviewContext
member.summary: Rebuilds what a menu backdrop is built from on a worker.
member.remarks:
Half of it is the title's — its content modules, its structural task types, its format profile and the service table its modules published — so a switch that left the old one standing would have the menu previewing the incoming game's levels through the outgoing game's content.
Its own step because of when it is possible: the detail maps and the lamp manifest it also carries are built later in start-up than the session is, and none of it is mutated afterwards, which is what makes it safe to hand to a worker.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.ShellMissions
member.summary: The campaign as the shell lists it, for the title running now.

remarks.para: The progression, not the browser order. Both are the catalogue's to define and they differ: the progression is the campaign exactly, while the browser order is everything the install holds with the campaign first. The screen this fills is headed CAMPAIGN, so it wants the former — and the distinction only started to matter when the sequel could be reached, because its browser order ends with six deathmatch maps and the screen offered them as missions 20 to 25.

Not the scan's order either, which is a directory walk and therefore alphabetical — it listed level 10 between level 1 and level 2. What the progression is, is the title's: one game chains each mission to the next and the other numbers them by location and level.

member.remarks: The one path F8, a rescan and a layer switched on or off all take. Reloading the RESOURCES is only half of it: everything already decoded from them -- an uploaded texture, the ground, the surface cache's baked diffuse -- holds its own copy, so those are rebuilt too, and only when something actually moved, because the reload is a visible hitch.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.ReloadTerrainTiles
member.summary: Puts the ground back up from whatever the resource registry now hands over.
member.returns: when the ground was re-uploaded.

remarks.para: A level's ground atlas is a LOOSE file, not an entry in an archive, and the two are replaced by different halves of the machinery: an archived texture is swapped in the registry and picked up by WorldRenderer.ReloadTextures, while a loose one is dropped from the registry and re-read on the next load. Nothing re-loads the ground by itself, because the atlas is decoded once when the level is built -- so without this the pack goes on and off every wall in the level and the ground underneath it never moves.
Only for a mission being PLAYED. A menu backdrop's terrain was built by the preview's own private registry, and the session's is not the one holding its bytes.

member.summary: Reports whether the camera has a roof over it, so the frame is drawn as an interior.

member.remarks: This used to be "inside the bounding box of a task named Building_", and that box is not the building: one standing at an angle to the world axes fills barely a third of it, so a quarter of the ground the test called indoors on mission one has open sky over it. member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.GameHost.BuildShelterField(OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldScene,OpenIGI.Game.World.LoadedMission)
member.summary: Builds the level's top-down map of what the solid world stands over, and binds it.
member.param: The mission's placed objects.
The mission whose models bend its spline segments, as the collision index bends them.

remarks.para: The one answer to "can the sky reach this point", for the fog, the falling rain, its splashes and the standing water alike. It is a raster of the collision geometry seen from above rather than a list of building bounding boxes, because the boxes were wrong both ways round: on mission one a quarter of the ground inside them has open sky over it — a building at an angle to the world axes fills barely a third of its own box — while two fifths of the ground genuinely under a roof lay outside every box, its shelter never having been labelled a building.
The CPU keeps the raster for its own questions and the GPU is handed a packed copy, so the puddle a pixel draws and the drop the storm culls are decided by the same numbers.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.DistanceFieldCache
member.summary: Reads and writes a level's baked signed distance fields to disk, so the structure the real-time lighting traces against is a build artifact loaded in a blink rather than re-derived every load.

remarks.para: The distance-field bake is the one thing standing between loading a mission and seeing it lit. calls it "a multi-second job" and runs it on a worker for exactly that reason — doing it on the thread holding a live GL context loses the context to the operating system's watchdog. But the lighting model cannot engage until the field exists, so the frame spends those seconds on the artists' baked lightmaps and then visibly crosses over to the real-time picture. That crossover is what this removes.

It is cacheable because it is the same answer every time. The fields are unsigned distances derived from static level geometry at a fixed voxel resolution: no sun, no time of day, no camera, nothing about how the level is being played. That makes it a stricter version of the bargain already trades on — the probe volume at least depends on the sun, and this does not depend on anything but the level and one integer.

So a file is keyed by the mission and the voxel resolution, plus a format version, and any change to those is a miss and a re-bake rather than a stale field silently loaded. That matters more here than it does for a probe volume: a wrong distance field is invisible in a rendered frame — it does not look wrong, it makes rays land on the wrong side of walls — and the only thing that would catch it is r_sdf_validate, which nobody runs by habit.

Only the fields and their placements are stored. The GPU atlas is rebuilt from them on load by , which is a pack and a copy rather than a trace — there is no point spending disk on something derived that cheaply, and it keeps the file free of anything that depends on the device it was written by.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.EmissiveLightProposer
member.summary: Works out which lights a level has, given that it declares none, and which of its surfaces are the lamps those lights come out of.

remarks.para: Two steps. works out which of the level's textures are light fixtures, from the shape and placement of the geometry that draws them; then turns every place one of those is drawn into a placed light with a position, a reach and a facing.

Both halves of the conclusion are used and both are written down. The fixtures become real lights in the deferred pass and real emitters in the surface cache's bounce; the emitter strengths go to the material library so that the lamp geometry ITSELF glows. Doing only the first is what made a room look lit by nothing — light on the floor with a grey panel above it.

A per-mission fixtures file, once written, is the truth: the detection ran once to propose the list and a human has had the chance to correct it since. Reading it also keeps the whole-level geometry walk and every texture decode off the load path entirely.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.GiBakeCache
member.summary: Reads and writes baked irradiance probe volumes to disk, so a level's global-illumination bake is a build artifact loaded in a blink rather than traced afresh every load.

remarks.para: The probe bake is the one part of a level load that blocks for seconds: the geometry question — what each probe can see — is expensive, and it is what the interactive load pumps and waits on. But the answer never changes, because the levels are static and the sun is a fixed direction per mission (that is the whole bargain the probe volume is built on). So it can be traced once, offline, and the result shipped: this cache is that result. A mission with a cached bake loads its lighting instantly; one without falls back to tracing it, and writes the result so the next load is fast too.

A cache file is keyed by the mission, the probe spacing and the sun direction it was baked under — the three inputs that decide the result — plus a format version, so a change to any of them is a miss and a re-bake, never a stale volume silently loaded. The payload (a few floats per probe, tens of thousands of probes) is gzip-compressed, which floats of gently-varying irradiance take well.

member.param: The lamp.

remarks.para: A roof alone is not a building. A walkway's canopy, a porch, the eave a wall lamp hangs under all have one, and the roof test kept every lamp under them burning at noon -- most of a camp's outdoor lights. What a room has that a canopy has not is walls: level rays from just under the lamp, all the way round, meet a wall inside a room and pass out from under a canopy. Glass and chain-link are seen through, as a line of sight sees through them: a fenced yard is not a room.
Where the world has no collision at all under the lamp -- a space drawn but not made solid -- the rays would leave every room, and the roof alone answers.

member.summary: Whether a lamp has a roof over it.
member.param: The lamp.
The roofs over the level.
member.returns: when most of the ground round it is covered, or when nothing can tell.

remarks.para: A ring round the lamp as well as the lamp itself, and most of them rather than any. The lamp's own point is not enough: a lantern's hood is solid and stands over it, and a lamp flush with a ceiling may have only the slab's thickness over it. A lamp on the outside of a wall sees the building over half its ring and open sky over the other half, and is outdoors, which it is.

With no roof raster -- a level that places nothing solid, or one not yet built -- every lamp answers as covered, which keeps it lit: a lamp left on in daylight is a far smaller wrong than a room gone dark at noon.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.LampShadowMaps
member.summary: Which lamps hold shadow maps, and drawing those maps.

remarks.para: Only where the device marches its lamp shadows rather than tracing them (see ). The lamps lighting the view take the map slots, nearest first, and keep them while they stay wanted, so a map is drawn once when its lamp arrives rather than every frame. A couple of slots are redrawn each frame in turn, which is how a soldier walking under a lamp comes to cast in it.

Every lamp takes six: a cube of ninety-degree views, as a point light's shadow is drawn -- from just in front of the glass for a fitting that faces a way, from its centre for one that does not. Whatever lies outside a lamp's maps falls to the distance-field march, which cannot hold a thin slab or tell a lamp's own housing from a wall, so the maps leave nothing in front of a lamp outside them.

member.remarks: Lamps whose light reaches into the view take the slots first, nearest first; the rest of the budget goes to those that do not, nearest first, so turning round finds their maps already drawn. Taken by distance alone, the lamps inside the rooms the player stood beside held every slot, and a floodlight over the door across the yard -- the one lighting what was on screen -- marched the distance field instead and lit the wall through the doorway, where the traced shadow had it dark.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.LampShadowMaps.LampMapView(OpenIGI.Game.World.LightFixture)
member.summary: Where a lamp's cube of maps is drawn from, and the projection each of its faces looks through.
member.param: The fixture.
member.returns: The camera's absolute position and the faces' shared projection.

remarks.para: A fitting that faces a way is drawn from a few centimetres in front of its glass. A single wide view out of the glass left everything beyond seventy-five degrees off its axis to the distance field, and that field cannot hold the slab a wall lamp is mounted just above: the wall and the ground under every such canopy lit in broad wedges, where the traced shadow had them dark. A cube sees the whole of the lamp's front, out to its own plane; what lies behind the glass is behind every face's near plane and reads as lit, and the lamp's own aim gives it no light.

One that does not is drawn from its centre, as a point light's cube is, with its near plane at three quarters of the fitting's size (five to thirty centimetres; five against a measured face). Nearer is the fitting's housing, which surrounds its centre: at three centimetres every face of the cube saw the box the bulb sits in, and a wall lamp shadowed the whole wall and the yard in front of it where the traced lamp lit them; at half its size the box's sides still stood inside the cube and cut a dark bow-tie along the wall either side of every lamp. Further loses the wall a room's lamp hangs a hand's breadth from: at the whole fitting's size, forty centimetres, a lamp thirty-five from the wall did not see it, and lit the air and the ground on its far side.

remarks.para: The hums vary least: a ballast hums at twice the mains frequency, and every one on a site shares the mains. The sparks and ticks vary most, being small parts that are never quite the same twice.

Every sound is normalised to the same peak, so the gains here are the mix. The hums carry several times the energy of a tick for a second or more, and are turned well down for it: what the ear should pick out of a dusk is the starters, with the ballasts a texture under them.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.MissionWarmUpGate
member.summary: Decides when a freshly loaded level may be shown: not after a fixed number of frames, but once the lighting it will be shown with exists, has converged, and has had a few frames to settle.

remarks.para: A load ending is not the same as a level being ready. The lighting model this renderer plays under is built rather than switched on -- a distance field that may still be baking on a worker, a surface cache that converges over dispatches -- and everything temporal on top of it needs frames. Counting frames alone, which is what the warm-up used to do, revealed a level whose field had not landed and let the player watch it cross over a few seconds later.

So this is a gate with three stages, each fed by the code that knows about it: the blocking load reports its stages, the lighting reports whether its structures are ready and how far the convergence has come, and the frame loop reports each drawn frame. The settle count starts only when the lighting is ready. Past a patience the gate opens anyway, because a hitch is better than a hang.
No device, no clock of its own: it is fed elapsed seconds, so it can be tested against every route a level takes in.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.PlayerFlashlight
member.summary: The player's flashlight: the switch, where the torch hangs and points, and handing it to the renderer.

remarks.para: Not retail. The original has no flashlight. It is the remaster's, on the Flashlight action (F by default), and it exists only where the renderer can light with it: r_flashlight, which vanilla pins off, and the deferred path, which vanilla does not draw. Where it cannot exist the key does nothing at all -- no light and no click -- so a vanilla run is the original and nothing else.

The torch hangs off the body rather than the camera: a hand's width to the right of the eye, a little below it and a little ahead, as a light clipped to a chest rig is. That offset is what makes its shadows visible at all -- a light at the eye casts every shadow straight behind what casts it -- and it stays with the body in third person, where the camera is somewhere else entirely. It aims where the crosshair lands, trails the view by a few hundredths of a second and sways with the gait ().

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.SurfaceCacheConvergence
member.summary: Solves a surface cache forward to its multi-bounce equilibrium a few slices at a time, so a level converges behind a loading screen or a held shot instead of in one multi-second stall.

remarks.para: The convergence itself is what it always was: one shadowed relight of the whole cache, a seed of the final atlas from it, and bounces folded in. Run back to back that measured two and a half seconds on the render thread for a large level -- a freeze, and one that landed mid-play whenever the distance field arrived after the level did. Divided into and stepped from the frame loop, the same work is spread over presented frames, so the window keeps answering, a progress bar can move, and a shot that is holding for it keeps drifting.

Paced by the GPU, not by the frame. The slices go out in batches, and a batch is not followed by another until the GPU has finished it: the work is marked as soon as it is recorded, and the marker polled from the frames after. How long the batch took to come back sizes the next one against , so a fast GPU is soon taking the maximum and a slow one settles at a slice at a time.

It used to size the step from how long the host's last frame took, doubling it under twelve milliseconds. But the host records a frame and moves on; until the frames in flight fill up, nothing it times includes the work it has queued. So every convergence opened by doubling blind -- two slices, four, eight, sixteen -- and on a MacBook Air's integrated GPU, a frame's command buffer carrying sixteen slices of shadowed, distance-field-traced lighting ran for seconds, which macOS answers by killing it and the device with it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.SurfaceCacheConvergence.Slices
member.summary: How many slices the cache is divided into.
member.remarks: Fine enough that one slice of the largest level is a few tens of milliseconds, coarse enough that a small level is not paying a hundred dispatches' worth of fixed cost. Sixteen puts the biggest measured cache at roughly 150 ms per slice per full pass.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.SurfaceCacheConvergence.BatchBudgetMilliseconds
member.summary: How long a batch may take to come back, recording to completion.
member.remarks: Measured from when the batch is recorded to the first frame that sees it finished, so it includes a frame or so of latency besides the batch's own GPU time. That makes it a conservative budget -- a batch is judged slower than it is -- and one a batch that has the GPU to itself still fits a frame within.

member.summary: How many slices the next batch takes, given how the last one went.

member.returns: As many as the budget affords at the last batch's cost per slice, at least one.

The cost per slice is measured from the whole batch, and a small batch is mostly the latency every batch pays, so it reads as cheaper per slice than a large one will be; taking the budget's word for it outright would jump from one slice to sixteen on the strength of a frame's worth of waiting. Shrinking is not held back: a batch that ran long is cut straight to what the budget affords, because the next one runs at that cost too.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionArming
member.summary: Makes the menu's backdrop ready to be played, a couple of milliseconds at a time, while the player is still looking at the menu.

remarks.para: A mission's level is built on a worker thread long before Play is pressed (), but the graphics work cannot leave the render thread: a mesh upload and a texture upload belong to the context that made them. That work is not large in total — it is large all at once, and a frame is what pays for it.

So it is done in pieces, under a time budget, on frames where the only thing happening is a menu. Every piece is one placement, one soldier, one weapon model: small enough that a single piece never overruns the budget on its own, which is the property the budget depends on, because a piece cannot be interrupted once it has started.

The largest single item by far is world residency. The backdrop's camera orbits one corner of the level, and the renderer resolves a model the first time it draws it — so most of the level is still unresolved when Play moves the camera to the player's spawn, and that one frame uploads the rest. Measured on mission 1 at about 260 ms. Walking every placement here turns that into nothing.
