member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionLoadSequence
member.summary: The presentation of going into a mission where no cinematic covers it: the picture the player was looking at freezes and falls out of focus as the interface leaves, a title card holds over it while the level is built and lit, and then the card leaves and the picture dissolves into the live level.

remarks.para: It owns no device and no renderer. A clock goes in, and every amount a frame needs -- how far out of focus, how much of the interface is left, where the card sits -- comes out, already eased. The game does two things on its say-so: captures the clean picture (before the interface is drawn over it) at the start, and runs the blocking load once the departure has played out, so the player watches the interface leave rather than a frozen menu. The hold then lasts exactly as long as the level needs.

The picture is the level itself -- the menu's backdrop of it, or the mission being restarted -- so what the player looks at while they wait is where they are going. The card is set in the shell's own faces and left-aligned, the way a title is: a caption over the place, not a dialog in front of it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionPreview
member.summary: A mission built for the menu backdrop, everything in it produced away from the graphics device and away from the running game, ready for the render thread to turn into renderers.

remarks.para: The point of this type is what it does not hold: no , no renderer, nothing owned by the GL context. Every field is plain data or a task tree, so all of it can be built on a worker; the handover on the render thread is then only the uploads, which is the part that genuinely has to happen there.

It carries its own and because that is what made the load safe to run in the background at all — see — and because a reads models and textures through the registry it was given for as long as it lives. Dropping the preview drops the whole context with it.

member.param: The mission this was built for.
The loaded mission: its descriptor, packs and terrain.

The private loop the level was built into: its task tree, its script namespace, its variables. Held because a preview is not only looked at — pressing Play promotes the backdrop into the played mission, and promotion is this loop becoming the game's own rather than the level being loaded a second time. A preview that is never promoted simply never has it advanced, which is what it was before.
The level's task tree, in the preview's own private tree.
The placements the world renderer draws.

The placements this title turns on the spot, or null when none do. Carried through the backdrop because a promoted mission IS the backdrop, and a fan that only turns when the mission was entered from the command line is the kind of difference nobody sees until they play from the menu.
The collision index built from those placements.
The terrain's material surface, or for a level with no usable terrain.

A packed detail map per ground tile, in tile order, derived on the worker. The single most expensive thing a backdrop swap used to do on the render thread; here it is already done and only wants uploading.
The places in the level worth circling behind the menu, the player's spawn first. Derived on the worker from where the level put its geometry — see .
The level's directional light, or when it declares none.
A shipped or cached probe field, or when the mission has no bake.
The registry the preview's packs were opened into; the world renderer reads through it.
The file system the preview's MISSION: alias is bound in.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionPreviewContext
member.summary: The pieces of the running session a menu backdrop needs in order to be promotable — that is, to become the played mission rather than be thrown away when the player presses Play.

remarks.para: A preview builds the whole level into its own private , and that privacy is what makes it safe to build on a worker thread. The consequence is that the level is built but not playable: nothing in that tree would ever tick, because the game advances a different loop. Promotion is the game changing which loop it advances, and for that to be possible the preview's loop has to have been built the way the session's own was.

So this carries the three things 's constructor takes that a look-only preview never needed — the wall clock, the flow host and the render scheduler — plus the archives that belong to the session rather than to any one level. Every one of them is either immutable or merely stored by the loop's constructor, so handing them to a worker makes no call on any of them.

member.param: The session's one wall clock. Both loops must read milliseconds from the same origin or every elapsed time in the frame loop jumps at the moment of the swap — see .
The flow host the loop reports state transitions to; stored, never called, on a preview.
The render scheduler the loop presents through; likewise only stored until promotion.
The shared Game_SetMission state. Its native has to exist in the promoted loop's namespace, or a level script that reaches for it after promotion would fault against a namespace that never had it.

The string archives read once at start-up — the menu's labels, the mission names and briefings, the handheld computer's three tables — as bytes. A promoted registry has to carry them because it becomes the registry everything resolves through, and reading them out of the session's own registry on a worker would be exactly the shared-state race the private context exists to avoid.

The installation's overrides folder — the store itself, which reports an empty index when there is no such folder, rather than a null standing for one. A preview builds the level into its own registry, and that registry becomes the game's own the moment Play is pressed — so a replacement pack that is not attached HERE is a folder that replaces nothing, however correctly it was built. The store is shared rather than copied: it is the session's one index of what is on disk, and a rescan from the console has to reach the registry the played mission resolves through.

The lamps a person named by hand, read once at start-up. A backdrop proposes its level's fixtures on the worker so the menu is lit the way the played mission will be, and the manifest is what the proposal is checked against.
The shipped and per-user distance-field caches. Read on the worker, so a cached field arrives with the backdrop rather than being loaded on the render thread after it; never written from there.

The session's derived detail-map pack. A backdrop's textures are decoded on a worker, and their maps are read there too rather than on the frame that uploads them; the pack is shared across missions, so this is the session's own and not the preview's.

The tables the playing session's content modules built. A preview registers the same modules into its own loop — the natives are per-loop and must be — but the tables are the session's, so a backdrop reads the magic-object table that is already loaded rather than a second, empty one.

The task types this title's editor emits no declaration for, so the loop registers them itself. It is the title's set and not a fixed one: what makes a type structural is that the title's own editor does not declare it, and the two games disagree by exactly one name — I.G.I. 2's editor declares Container with a parameter, and a loop that had registered it with none refuses every level that mentions it.
Which encodings this title's assets may hold. Without it a pack is read as the first game's, and a title shipping a later mesh version has every model refused while the pack still opens.
The running title's content modules. A preview registers the same ones into its own loop, so its tree comes out shaped the way the scene walk expects rather than as untyped placeholders.

The running title's scene walk. A backdrop is promoted into the played mission and keeps the scene it walked, so a preview that used a different walk from the mission's would not merely look wrong — it would become the mission's world. This used to call the first game's walk by name, which for the sequel placed almost nothing and said nothing about it.
Whether the device can run compute at all. A distance field is only ever traced against on a device that can, so a backdrop built for one that cannot should not spend a worker baking one.
Whether the device samples block-compressed textures, so a texture pack's stored chains are kept as they are rather than expanded on the worker.
Which game the backdrop belongs to, as GameTitle.Id gives it. It names the mission's fixture file, and the two titles number their missions independently over ranges that overlap.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionPreviewLoader
member.summary: Builds the menu's backdrop mission on a worker thread and hands the result to the render thread when it is ready, so browsing the campaign never stalls the frame.

remarks.para: Why a level load could not simply be moved onto a thread. Loading a mission rebinds the file system's MISSION: alias, registers the level's packs into a resource registry, and builds a task tree by running scripts against a namespace of natives and variables. In the game those three are one each, shared, and the render thread is reading all of them — ticking the live level's tasks, resolving its models — every frame. A worker doing the same work would be rebinding an alias and mutating a tree out from under it. That is the reason only ever pulled the files into the operating system's cache: reading a file races nothing.

What makes it safe here. Each preview load gets its own file system, resource registry and task tree — a private whose only purpose is to own a and a namespace, and which is never advanced. Nothing the worker writes is visible to the running game, so there is nothing to race. What it does share is read-only and finished being written at start-up: the mission table and the magic-object table are dictionaries nothing mutates after the initial scan, and the probe cache is read, not written. A backdrop needs no ticking anyway — it is static geometry under a slow orbit — so the private tree is simply never run.

What is left on the render thread. Only the uploads: a GL texture belongs to the context that made it, so the terrain's tiles, the sky and the world renderer are built in GameHost when the result is collected. That is the same handover and DistanceFieldBake already use.

A request supersedes whatever was in flight: the worker's result carries the mission it was for, and a result nobody is waiting for any more is dropped rather than swapped in. There is no way to interrupt a load part-way, so a superseded one is left to finish and discarded — it costs a worker thread for a moment and never touches the game.

member.param: The installation to read from.
The mission table, complete and read-only after the start-up scan.
The magic-object table, likewise read-only after start-up.
The shipped and per-user probe caches, read for a mission's baked lighting.
The authored orbit styles each mission's showcase points are based on.
What a built preview needs to be promotable into the played mission.
The logger.
Where a backdrop is built: beside the menu where the platform can, and inline -- a stall on the frame that asks -- where it cannot.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionPreviewLoader.DeriveGroundDetailAsync(OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainData)
member.summary: Derives every ground tile's detail map, the tiles in parallel with one another.
member.param: The level's terrain, or when it has none to speak of.
member.returns: A packed detail map per tile in tile order, or an empty set when there are no tiles.

remarks.para: A ground tile has no name to look a shipped map up by, so one is derived from its pixels — and that derivation is the better part of a second across a level's tiles, far and away the largest single cost in building a backdrop. Each tile is derived from nothing but its own pixels into its own array, so there is no shared state at all and the work divides perfectly.

One core is deliberately left free. The whole point of this class is that a backdrop is built without the game stuttering, and taking every core to do it would cost the render thread exactly what moving the work off it was meant to save.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Menu.MissionWarmer
member.summary: Warms a mission's data on a worker thread when the campaign carousel hovers it, so the level it will load is already in the operating system's file cache by the time the player presses Play.

remarks.para: True two-scene streaming — a second live world cross-fading in behind the menu — is more than the single-scene render loop offers, and mutating the task tree from a worker is not safe. What is both safe and useful is this: on hover, cancel the previous warm and start reading the hovered mission's files off disk on a thread-pool thread. It touches no shared state (plain reads), never blocks the UI thread, and turns the eventual synchronous load into a warm-cache one. The visible hand-off is the shell's own cross-fade; the data is what streams.
The read is cancellable and best-effort: a hover that moves on before the read finishes cancels it, and any I/O error is swallowed — a warm that fails just means the real load pays full price.

does the same for every mission, one after another, once the menu is up: the first backdrop of each mission then reads from memory however far down the list the player jumps. A hover outranks it -- the sweep stops while the hovered mission is read and picks up after it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.RendererSwitch
member.summary: Where the game picks up again once the other renderer has been built.
member.param: The mission being played, or nought for the menu.
The time of day and weather the campaign screen chose for it.

The hour to light the level at, as r_time_of_day takes it: 0 to 24, or negative for the level's own authored sun. Carried apart from the campaign's choice because the hour is set in more places than that -- the settings menu, the console, a day that has been running -- and the switch has to come back to the same sky whichever it was.
Where the player stood or the free camera hung, or null for the mission's own start.
The last picture the switched-from renderer presented, or null where none was read.
The API to build next, where r_renderer named one; null for the next in the switch key's order.
The menu section to open on when there is no mission to resume, or null for the landing page.
member.remarks:
A renderer is not swapped under a running game: every texture, mesh and pipeline the game holds was made by the one it has, and the host keeps them for the life of a level. So the game is ended, the other renderer is built on the same window, and a new game starts the same mission and puts the player back -- the same load a mission start costs, and what it restores is what a look at the picture needs: the place, the facing and the hour. Progress through the mission is not carried over.
The load is not shown. The switched-from renderer's last picture is held on screen, exactly as it was, until the new one reveals the level, so the eye goes from one renderer's picture straight to the other's -- which is what comparing them needs, and what a loading screen between them destroys.

member.summary: Opens the audio backend, the bank and the score, and levels the buses.

remarks.para: Called once, after the console has read settings.cfg and the command line's +statements, because the voice count and the output rate are fixed when the device opens. The volumes are not -- those are pushed on change through .
A backend that cannot open is not an error. The factory returns a silent device rather than throwing, so there is nothing here to handle: the game runs either way.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.AudioOutput.ApplyCategoryGains
member.summary: Pushes the volume variables onto the device's buses.
member.remarks: The master gain is folded into each bus rather than applied separately, because the device model has one gain per bus and no master of its own -- the original has no master either, only the three per-profile volumes.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.AudioOutput.Advance
member.summary: Advances the device and the score, once a frame.
member.returns: The wall-clock seconds since the last advance; zero on the first.
member.remarks: The fade is driven from the wall clock rather than from ticks. A fade is presentation, and tying it to the simulation would make it lurch whenever the loop catches up on a backlog of ticks.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.AudioOutput.ResetForMission
member.summary: Stops the score, frees the buffers, and empties the bank down to the menu's sounds.

remarks.para: Called before each mission load, so the mission's own directory is mounted into a bank holding only the menu sounds. The original rebuilds its table the same way; leaving the previous level's sounds in place would let a name resolve to a sound the new level never shipped.

Clearing is the only thing that can retire a name, because the bank keeps the FIRST mount of one -- faithfully, since the original's loader reports "SOUND - File %s already loaded!" rather than replacing. Every mission ships its own sounds/game_music.wav, and a mounted entry holds the path it was found at rather than the mission alias it was found through, so a bank carried across a load answers game_music with the previous level's score forever.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.AudioOutput.ForgetDefinitions
member.summary: Forgets the definitions, as the title changes.
member.remarks: They are loaded per mission from the title's own resources, and only builds a registry when there is none -- so a registry carried across a switch would hand the incoming game the outgoing one's names.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Services.CutsceneSkipHold
member.summary: The hold that skips a cutscene: the break key held down long enough, with how far it has got for the ring that shows it.

remarks.para: The original skipped on the break key's first press, which a player reaching for the pause menu as a mission opens, or a thumb landing on a phone's screen, set off by accident. Here the key has to be held for ; let go early and the ring drains again. Both titles' cutscenes go through it: the host's own (Project I.G.I.'s level cutscenes) break when reports the hold complete, and a title player's read as their break key, held from then until the cutscene has ended, as the original's scripts expect to see it.
A key still held when one cutscene has been skipped does not go on to skip the next: it has to be let go first.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Services.GlobalIllumination.EffectiveLighting
member.summary: The lighting model the frame may actually use, which is the one asked for only once the structures it lights from exist.

remarks.para: dynamic DISCARDS the artists' bakes: it does not sample an object lightmap at all. Everything it puts in their place — the screen probe gather, the world radiance cache, the lamps — reads the surface cache and the distance field, and both of those are built rather than switched on. So the instant between asking for dynamic lighting and having something to light with is a frame with the bakes thrown away and nothing yet to replace them: a flat, wrong picture.

That instant used to be permanent. r_cards and r_sdf were RequiresRestart and built only during a mission load, so choosing Ultra from the settings menu mid-session — or moving the Global Illumination row — asked for a lighting model whose inputs could not arrive until the player restarted the game. Nothing said so; the frame simply went flat.

Reading the model through here instead makes the switch safe from both ends. starts building the moment the model is asked for, and until it finishes this reports — so the frame keeps the lighting it already had and crosses over when there is something better to cross to. There is never a wrong frame, only an early one.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Services.GlobalIllumination.Ready
member.summary: Whether everything the dynamic model lights from is built and usable.
member.remarks: Both structures, not either: a gather with a distance field and no surface cache traces to a hit it cannot read the colour of, and one with a cache and no field cannot find the hit at all. The device check is the same one the builders make — without compute there is no field to build, so a level loaded on such a device stays on the bakes however the preset is set.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Services.GlobalIllumination.Wanted
member.summary: Whether the frame wants the dynamic model at all, on a device that could run it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Services.GlobalIllumination.Pending
member.summary: Whether anything the dynamic model needs is still on its way: a field baking or not yet attempted, a cache not yet captured, or a convergence that has not finished.
member.remarks: This is what a loading screen waits on. It is deliberately "still coming" rather than "not ready": a level whose capture found nothing, or whose bake produced nothing, is not going to change, and a gate that waited for it would hold a panel over a level that was as lit as it would ever be.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.GlobalIllumination.EnsureStructures
member.summary: Builds whatever the real-time lighting model needs and does not yet have, and throws away whatever it no longer needs.

remarks.para: Called once a frame from the render loop as well as during a mission load, which is what lets the settings menu turn real-time global illumination on in a running level. The work is the same work the load does; only its trigger is new.

The costs are not symmetrical and it matters which is which. The distance-field bake is a worker thread that the loop already polls, so asking for it mid-session costs nothing on the frame it is asked for. The surface-cache capture is a render pass over every distinct model and cannot be anything else — the atlas is a framebuffer and the geometry belongs to this context — so it lands as one long frame. That is a visible hitch, and it is the honest price of the switch; it is logged so that a hitch nobody asked about can be explained afterwards.

A backdrop counts. The menu's level used to be a picture and never gathered, which meant it was lit by the artists' bakes while the mission it became was lit by the real-time model -- and the picture changed the moment Play was pressed. Building the structures for the backdrop too is what makes the menu show the level the player is about to be standing in.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.GlobalIllumination.ApplyLamps(OpenIGI.Host.Lighting.EmissiveLightProposer.Proposal,System.Int32)
member.summary: Puts a level's proposed lamps into every place that reads them.
member.param: The level's fixtures and glowing geometry, or none.
The mission they belong to, which seeds the switchboard.
member.remarks: The lamps a level implies but never declares, used in three places: as EMISSION on the fixture geometry itself, so a lamp looks like the thing doing the lighting; as real lights in the deferred pass, so a windowless room has a source at all; and as emitters the surface cache bounces off, where there is one. All three matter together -- a room lit from a fixture that does not glow reads as lit by nothing, and a fixture that glows without lighting reads as a decal. Shared by the backdrop and the played mission, so a promoted level keeps the lamps its backdrop was already showing rather than surveying them a second time.

member.remarks: The fault and the switch are two separate facts about a fitting — a lamp can be switched off AND have a dying tube in it, and turning it back on will show that — so both are reported rather than one standing in for the other.
The daylight is a third: a lamp switched on at the wall that its photocell has put out for the day is on and dark, and says so.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.LevelLamps.TryAimedLamp(OpenIGI.Game.World.LampSwitchboard,System.Int32@,System.Double@)
member.summary: Finds the lamp the frame's own eye is looking at, with the level's walls respected.
member.param: The level's lamps.
Receives the fixture's index.
Receives how far away it is, in metres.
member.returns: when a lamp is under the crosshair and nothing is in front of it.

remarks.para: Cast from host.Eye, which is the pose the last frame was drawn from whichever camera claimed it. That is one frame stale, which is exactly nothing for a key press: a person aiming at a lamp is holding still on it.

The occlusion test is the level's own collision rather than anything the lamps know about, because a wall is not in the fixture list and never will be. Without it the crosshair reaches lamps in the next room, and a key press switches off a light nobody can see change — which reads as the key doing nothing.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.LevelLamps.Update(System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Advances every lamp, and lets the bounce catch up with them.
member.param: The loop's real-time clock.
Whether what the lamps do is to be heard: a level being played, not a backdrop.

remarks.para: Real elapsed time rather than the tick, and on every pass of the loop rather than every rendered frame, for the same reason the camera and the day/night sweep are: a fade tied to the frame rate is a different fade on a different machine, and a lamp striking is a tenth of a second of shape that a coarse step walks straight over.

The surface cache's emitters are a storage buffer, so they are re-uploaded when the board says something moved and not otherwise — a level nobody has touched never uploads at all, and a flickering tube's bounce trails its own glow by a frame or two, which is invisible against a bounce that takes far longer than that to converge in the first place.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Host.Services.LevelLamps.NearestOrder
member.summary: Gets the fixtures the last chose, nearest first.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.LevelLamps.SelectNearest(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Single)
member.summary: Chooses which of the level's lamps this frame submits, nearest first.
member.param: Where the camera stands, in world metres.
Unused by the ranking; see the remarks on why it must not scale it.
member.returns: How many entries of are valid.

remarks.para: A level's lamps outnumber the shader's array several times over, so this is a choice and not a truncation. Each fixture is ranked by how far OUTSIDE its own reach the camera stands: a lamp the camera is inside ranks negative and always makes the cut, and beyond that a long fluorescent batten twenty metres off beats a desk lamp fifteen metres off, which is the right way round because reach is what decides whether a lamp can light anything the player can see.
The camera's own position rather than the frustum: a lamp behind the player still lights the wall in front of them, and culling to what is on screen would switch that light off as they turned.

A running insertion into an array of thirty-two rather than a sort of the whole list. The list is a few hundred long and this runs every frame; an insertion sort over a fixed, tiny destination is linear in the input and allocates nothing, where sorting the input is neither.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.MemoryDiagnostics.TrimAfterLoad
member.summary: Gives back what a finished load leaves idle: upload staging, and the large-object heap's holes.
member.remarks: Called under the held frame of a backdrop swap, where a collection's pause is not seen. A level's worth of decoded pictures has just gone through the large-object heap, which the collector does not compact unless asked -- the holes they leave are memory the process keeps. The browser's runtime (Mono) has no such heap and throws PlatformNotSupportedException for any mode but Default, so there the collection runs without it.

member.param: The world's renderer, whose decode cache holds every picture it decoded.
The material detail maps, whose unclaimed entries go.
member.remarks: The decode cache holds every picture it decoded until the renderer takes it; whatever the level never drew stays there for as long as the level does. Once the level is resident nothing more will be taken, so the rest goes, and the staging that carried the uploads with it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.MenuBackdrop.IsLite(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Gets whether the level on screen is the menu's backdrop and is to be drawn without the preset's expensive parts. See .
member.param: Whether a mission is being played.
member.returns: for the lite profile.
member.remarks: A backdrop is the level when no mission is: the preview is dropped the moment one is promoted or a mission loads cold, so Play turns this off on the same frame the level becomes the mission.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.MenuBackdrop.UpdateProfile(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Applies or clears the lite profile to match . Cheap; call freely.
member.param: Whether a mission is being played.

remarks.para: What the lite profile removes is everything a backdrop swap had to BUILD on the render thread -- the surface-cache capture, which ends in a device wait, and the distance-field upload -- and the per-frame work whose only output is detail the blur takes away: shadows, traces and screen-space gathers. The level then draws on its own bakes, which is what it looked like before any of that.

Through overrides rather than assignments, deliberately. These are preset-managed, archived variables: writing them would flip the preset to Custom while the menu is up and save the menu's numbers as the player's own the next time the settings are written. An override is seen only by the code reading Value.

Clearing it is all Play has to do. The per-frame sees the structures wanted again and builds them, and the mission's warm-up holds the picture until they are ready (), so the cost moves behind the going-in sequence.
Nothing in a lite backdrop traces, so nothing is admitted to the traced world either: every mesh it took in would be a structure built for a level that is gone at the next swap.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.MenuFlow.DrawDissolve(OpenIGI.UI.UiPainter,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Draws the held frame over the live one, so the two cross-dissolve.
member.param: The shell's painter, which draws over the resolved scene and under the menu.
The window's width.
The window's height.
member.remarks: The renderer keeps one live world, so two levels can never be on screen at once. What can be is the last frame of the outgoing one: it is held as a texture and faded off over the incoming level, which is a true dissolve rather than a dip through black. The camera's orbit is slow enough that a still is indistinguishable from the live picture over a third of a second.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Host.Services.SurfaceCacheResidency.GiSunFollowSlices
member.summary: How many slices of the whole cache the far refresh relights a frame while the sun is moving.
member.remarks: Three rather than eight. Each slice is a relight and a bounce of a 128th of the whole level, about one and a half milliseconds at ultra, and eight of them took the frame from a hundred frames a second to thirty-three for as long as the scrub key was held. Three keep a whole pass inside a second at sixty, still quicker than the scrub crosses dusk.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Host.Services.SurfaceCacheResidency.FarRefreshQuietRounds
member.summary: How many whole sweeps the far refresh runs after its inputs last changed, before it idles.
member.remarks: One sweep relights every card under the new inputs; the rest fold more bounce in, at the steady bounce's weight, so far rooms reach their multi-bounce answer rather than stopping at one. At the ultra preset's 128 slices this is about eight seconds at sixty frames a second.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Host.Services.SurfaceCacheResidency.GiSettleTimeoutFrames
member.summary: The longest the convergence waits for the traced world to stop growing, in frames.
member.remarks: Ten seconds at sixty. A level that never settles -- something keeps arriving at the edge of the admission radius -- converges against what it has rather than not at all, and the refresh sweep corrects it as the rest arrives.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.SurfaceCacheResidency.BeginConvergence
member.summary: Starts solving the surface cache forward to its multi-bounce equilibrium, so a level opens at the lighting it settles on rather than climbing towards it in front of the player.

remarks.para: Two separate ramps are being collapsed here, and the direct one is the bigger of the two. In the steady state the shadowed relight walks the cache a slice at a time over r_gi_amortize frames -- that spread is what keeps a clipmap scroll from stalling the frame -- so a level that simply starts running opens with its cards lit but UNSHADOWED and darkens as the slices arrive. The convergence relights the whole cache once, with a field to trace shadows against.

The second is the bounce, which is a progressive solve: each pass folds one more bounce into the last one's result at a weight of one over one plus the pass. Doing those passes one a frame in front of the player is the visible "lighting up".

The whole cache rather than the active radius, deliberately. The radius exists to keep the STEADY-STATE refresh off cards the player is nowhere near, and it is centred on the camera -- which at this point in a load is not yet where the player will stand. Converging the level once costs a bounded amount of load time and means walking somewhere new does not re-run the ramp.

Started here and STEPPED by from the frame loop, rather than run to completion: as one call it measured two and a half seconds on a large level, and it ran whenever the second half of the pair landed, which on a cold cache was several seconds into play. Spread over frames the same work goes on behind the loading screen, or under the held shot, while the picture keeps presenting. A lockstep capture still runs it in one go, because a capture has to be the same frame every time.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.SurfaceCacheResidency.StepConvergence
member.summary: Runs this frame's share of the convergence, if one is in flight. Once per frame.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.SurfaceCacheResidency.StepRelight
member.summary: Refreshes one slice of the WHOLE cache, direct light and one bounce, every frame.

remarks.para: The steady-state refresh only reaches cards within r_gi_cache_radius of the camera, and the load-time convergence runs once. So whatever the far cards were converged under stayed there: a world structure still filling in (walls not yet admitted, and so not in anyone's shadow), a clock that has moved on, lamps that arrived or were switched after it. The player saw it put right only by walking up to each place in turn.

The cache is kept current with a per-frame budget of card updates over the whole scene rather than a radius around the eye: the whole cache is swept a slice a frame, the direct term relit under this frame's sun and lamps and a bounce folded in at half weight, so a far surface follows every change within a few seconds and never pops -- both halves blend. The slices near the camera are refreshed twice, which costs little and changes nothing.
Relighting the direct term alone, as this first did, changed nothing anyone could see: the far cards show the FINAL atlas, which only the bounce writes, and the steady bounce is radius-culled too.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.AmbientSkyLight
member.summary: The sky's light averaged over every direction, as the lighting pass itself has it.
member.returns: The radiance a white diffuse surface would send back if the sky lit it from all round, with r_sky_light already in it; the flat fill where the renderer has no sky to report.

remarks.para: For what hangs in the air rather than sits on a surface -- a falling drop is lit from every side. Taken from the same harmonics the deferred lighting and the fog read, averaged over the sphere: the linear terms' constants, and a third of the z-squared term, the only quadratic one whose average is not nought.

Not the level's flat ambient. That is what the renderer fell back on before it had a sky, and at night it is several times the light the scene is actually lit by -- which is what drew every rain streak brighter than the ground it fell past, and a rainy night as a wall of rain.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.DaylightColour(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Re-points a light's colour to a target chromaticity while keeping its own luminance.
member.remarks: The level's authored light colours carry the game's stylised warmth; this swaps the HUE for a physical daylight one -- a near-white sun, a cool-blue sky -- without touching how BRIGHT the level asked the light to be. The target is scaled by the ratio of the source's luminance to its own, so a dim ambient stays dim and a strong sun stays strong; only the balance between the channels changes.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.WarmedAmbient(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Single)
member.summary: Warms a level's cool zenith ambient towards the horizon as the sun sinks.
member.remarks: The sky an interior sees at a low sun is the warm horizon, not the cool zenith: the atmosphere reddens as the sun sinks and a real skylight carries that warmth into the room. The level ships a single cool ambient triple with no notion of the sun's height, so read literally it leaves a dusk-lit room as flatly blue as a noon one. This blends it towards a golden horizon tint by how low the sun sits -- keeping its own brightness so only the hue shifts -- and fades the warmth out above a moderate elevation, where the ambient is left alone. Applied at the source so both the deferred ambient and the GI sky fill inherit it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.SkyWarmthTint(System.Single)
member.summary: A per-channel tint for the sky dome that reddens towards the horizon as the sun sinks.
member.param: The sine of the sun's elevation; 1 is overhead, negative is below the horizon.
member.remarks: The authored sky is a fixed blue with no sense of the sun's height. A low sun scatters the blue out of the light that reaches the ground and leaves the horizon warm, so this multiplies the dome towards a warm tint by how low the sun sits -- one at a high sun, so a noon sky is the authored blue untouched. It is the sky counterpart to : together they warm both what a window shows and what the fill carries in.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.CycleSun
member.summary: The sun -- or the moon -- the level is lit by at the cycle's current hour.

remarks.para: One answer for everything that lights the level, because two answers is how the level ended up lit twice. The frame used to derive its sun inline while the surface cache converged under EffectiveSun ?? Sun -- and during a load the first is not set yet, so the second, the level's raw authored Dirlight, lit the whole cache. Every Project I.G.I. mission authors that as a NOON sun, so a night mission's every distant surface was converged in daylight and stayed that way: the steady refresh only reaches cards near the camera, so a tunnel across the valley glowed until the player walked up to it.

A pinned sun (-sundir) keeps the level's own colour with the pinned direction. Otherwise the level's bound sun is swept to the hour; a title that leaves its fill to the renderer has its ambient re-pointed to a daylight chroma by day; and under cloud the moon loses most of its directional light to the deck.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.MoonVeil
member.summary: How much of the moon's light is left once the weather and r_moonlight have had it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.WeatherCloudCover
member.summary: How overcast the sky is, as far as the night is concerned: a raining or snowing level is.
member.remarks: The level's own weather decides it, through the same flag the rain's draw and sound read, not whether the storm is drawing this frame. That one goes off whenever the camera steps under a roof, and the sky outside does not clear because the player went indoors.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Host.Services.TimeOfDayLighting.FrameNightSky
member.summary: What the night sky holds this frame beyond the atmosphere: glow, cover, stars and moon.
member.remarks: Everything is weighted by how far into night the cycle is, so a day, or a capture with a pinned sun, carries none of it and draws exactly the sky it always did.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Titles.TitleBinding
member.summary: Everything the host needs in order to run one game, resolved together.
member.param: The title's layout, format profile and content modules.
The renderers it draws its world with.
How a loaded level becomes placements.
Builds the title's own mission table; a factory, because the scan logs as it goes.
Where this title is installed, or empty when it is not.
The title's own player, or for a title that walks the host's rig.

remarks.para: Four lookups that used to be four constructor parameters, resolved one title at a time. Bundling them is not tidiness: the host can now be handed a different title's four while it is running, and a switch that took three of the four would be a game drawing one title's world through another's renderers.

They stay four separate things rather than one interface because the reference graph forbids joining them — Engine cannot name a WorldScene and so cannot carry the walk, and Presentation references Engine and so cannot be named by it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Host.Titles.ITitleCatalog
member.summary: The games a build can run, and where each of them is.

remarks.para: Implemented by the composition root, which is the only place allowed to name more than one title. The host takes this rather than one title's pieces so that switching games at run time is the same operation as starting in one — there is no second path that could get a different answer.

It is deliberately not a registry the host can add to. A title is a compile-time fact about which content assemblies were linked, and discovering them by reflection would cost the AOT targets their static call graph for a list that is three lines long.
